correctness.rationale: The full primary source was inspected for the nonstandard premise that a nontrivial positive two-cycle has squarefree members with disjoint prime supports. For such members, the two logarithmic derivatives are positive reciprocal-prime sums A and B with AB=1, so A+B>=2. Among N distinct primes the reciprocal sum is maximized by the first N primes. Exact rational arithmetic gives the first-58-prime sum below 2, forcing N>=59. The packaged verifier regenerates all data using integer arithmetic.

Kovic develops the same ordinary arithmetic-derivative two-cycle problem and proves the published unconditional total-support lower bound 34.
Kovic additionally proves conditional total-support bounds 57 and 110 under exclusions of small primes.

originality.rationale: Kovic Proposition 18 is the closest statement and proves total support at least 34, with conditional bounds 57 when both members are odd and 110 when neither 2 nor 3 occurs. The new 59 bound is unconditional. Ufnarovski--Ahlander supply the cycle reduction and product-one reciprocal equation but not this threshold. No equivalent 59-support result was found in the checked research records or statement-level literature searches.
residual_risks: A short unpublished or unindexed note may already combine the product-one reciprocal formulation with the first-prime reciprocal threshold.
No nontrivial positive arithmetic-derivative two-cycle is known, so the theorem is a necessary condition for a hypothetical object.
The bound 59 is not claimed optimal among all possible arguments; it is only the exact threshold of the combined reciprocal-sum obstruction.

value.rationale: The existence of nontrivial arithmetic-derivative cycles is an explicit archival open problem, and the closest paper develops prime-support lower bounds as its main quantitative progress. The new argument raises the unconditional total-support barrier from 34 to 59 and the forced support of one member from 17 to 30. It is a structural improvement with an exact finite certificate, not a routine bounded enumeration.
